punchline: In Tetlock's study, which Taleb describes, experts with big reputations made worse predictions than those nobody had heard of.
thirty_sec: Taleb describes a test where people give a range they're 98 percent sure about. They should miss 2 percent of the time. They miss close to 45 percent. Then there's Philip Tetlock, who collected about 27,000 predictions from nearly 300 experts. They were wrong far more than they thought, and the famous ones did worse. Taleb's advice: prepare instead of predict. Tetlock later did find a few forecasters who beat chance on short questions.
